opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, especially when we're hiring or deciding who should lead a new direction.

A strong engineer, given a well-specified problem, will get it done fast, robustly, and at scale. That's incredibly valuable; honestly, a lot of progress in this field comes down to really excellent engineering. But research taste is about the step before that: picking which problem is worth solving at all, and having a good prior on what's likely to work before you've spent the compute to find out.

A few things stand out in people with great taste. First, they're good at telling what's a real signal and what's noise. You run an experiment, you see a small bump, and the person with taste knows whether to chase it or whether it's a seed-variance artifact. They have good instincts about which results will survive scaling and which ones are just a trick at small scale.

Second, they're willing to be stubborn in the right places and flexible in the right places. Some of the most important bets look bad for a long time. Someone with taste can hold conviction on an idea through a lot of negative results because they have a clear model of *why* it should work, but they'll also drop an idea quickly when the evidence says their model was wrong. That calibration is hard to teach.

Third, they ask simple questions. Often the best researchers aren't the ones proposing the most elaborate method. They're the ones who say, "What's the simplest thing that could possibly explain this?" or "What happens if we just scale this up?" There's a kind of aesthetic toward simplicity and generality that tends to pay off.

And I'd say the line between the two isn't fixed. Many of the best researchers I know started as very strong engineers, and that's where they built their intuition, because they ran thousands of experiments and saw what actually moves the needle. Taste comes from contact with reality. So if someone wants to develop it, my advice is to run a lot of experiments, write down your predictions beforehand, and check how often you were right. That feedback loop is how you build it.

r001.rationale: It describes research taste as choosing which problems are worth pursuing and judging what is likely to work before the evidence is clear.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing directions and evaluating evidence, but does not identify persuading others that a direction is promising as part of research taste.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because at OpenAI we've hired a lot of people who come from both backgrounds, and honestly some of the best researchers we have started out as engineers.

The way I'd put it is that research taste is really about knowing which problems are worth working on, and which approaches are likely to pay off, before you have the evidence. A strong engineer is often very good at execution. You give them a well-specified problem and they'll build the thing, they'll make it fast, they'll make it reliable. That's incredibly valuable, and I don't want to downplay it at all, because in modern AI research, a huge amount of the progress is really engineering progress.

But research is different in that the problem is usually not well specified. You're sitting there with a hundred things you could try, and most of them won't work. And taste is the thing that lets you say, okay, these three are the ones that matter, and here's the experiment that would actually tell me something. It's about being able to have a model of why something would work, not just trying stuff. A lot of it is also knowing when to stop. Engineers tend to want to make the thing work, and sometimes the right research call is, this isn't going anywhere, abandon it and go do something else.

The other piece is that good researchers are kind of obsessed with the question of what is the simplest version of this that would still teach me something. There's a tendency, especially when you have a lot of compute, to just scale everything up and see. But the people with real taste can run a tiny experiment and extract most of the signal from it, because they've thought hard about what the experiment is actually testing.

What's interesting is I don't think taste is some innate thing. You develop it by being wrong a lot. The researchers I trust the most have usually spent years running experiments that failed and slowly built up intuitions about what the failure modes look like. So part of what we try to do is give people room to build that, to let them pursue things that might not work, because that's how you get there.

And I'd say the ideal person, especially today, is really both. The research directions that are winning right now require you to be able to reason carefully about what to try and also to actually go build the infrastructure to try it at scale. The people who can do both are rare, and they're the ones who end up driving the big results.

r001.rationale: The response describes research taste as choosing which problems and approaches are worth pursuing before evidence is available, especially when many options exist and the problem is poorly specified.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing and testing research directions, but does not identify persuading others that a direction is promising as part of research taste.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is largely about choosing the right problem and figuring out which uncertainties are worth spending time on. In engineering, you can often start with a fairly clear objective, and the challenge is executing really well. In research, part of the work is discovering what the objective should be and whether your approach has a chance of getting you there.

A strong researcher might look at a result that seems disappointing and say, “Actually, there’s something interesting here. We should understand why this happened.” Or they might look at a result that seems promising and realize it’s coming from something incidental. That judgment—knowing what to pursue and what to let go—is a big part of taste.

But I don’t think there’s a sharp boundary. Being a strong engineer lets you test ideas quickly, and that feedback is how you develop research taste. You build intuition by making predictions, running experiments, and being honest when the results don’t match what you expected.

r001.rationale: It describes research taste as choosing the right problem and deciding what to pursue when the objective and likelihood of success are uncertain.

r002.rationale: It discusses judging which directions are worth pursuing, but does not identify persuading others that a direction is promising as part of research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of research taste as knowing which uncertainty is worth spending your time on. A strong engineer can take a goal and find a reliable way to achieve it. A strong researcher also has to ask whether that’s the right goal, whether the assumptions behind it hold, and what experiment would actually change their mind.

There’s a balance there. You want to pursue something ambitious enough that it matters, but concrete enough that you can get feedback. Sometimes the best next experiment is very small—it just cleanly separates two explanations for what you’re seeing.

And I wouldn’t draw too sharp a line between the two. Good engineering lets you test ideas quickly and trust the results. That feedback is a big part of how you develop taste: you make a prediction, run the experiment, and learn where your intuition was wrong.

r001.rationale: It frames research taste as deciding “which uncertainty is worth spending your time on” and asking whether a goal and its assumptions are right, including choosing experiments when the path is unclear.
